messages.subject: Horseshoe effect in gmPCA?
messages.body_plain:
In helping a colleague with their analysis, I see that their PCA has a noticeable horseshoe/arch effect in it (see below). I recall learning that such an effect can imply that PC2 is simply a distortion of PC1, and/or non-linearity across whatever gradient is measured. Seeing as these are GPA shape coordinates, I'm not sure how to interpret the issue or go about resolving it. Any help is appreciated.
-Russ

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Horseshoe effect in gmPCA?
messages.body_plain:
Russ,

Yes, some ecologists in the earlier literature did claim the horseshoe/arch effect was a ‘distortion’; though to my mind that was largely due to the incorrect expectation that samples obtained along an ecological gradient should result in a linear path in the multivariate space. It was found most common in community composition data, and was best explained as the phasing in and out of different species along the gradient (for those interested, see Legendre and Legendre’s Numerical Ecology textbook for an explanation and simple simulation demonstrating the effect).

As to finding this in shape data, I find this really quite interesting. What I would suggest here for interpreting the pattern is to generate hypothetical shapes along the arch to get a sense of how shapes change along it. This can be done with shape.predictor/plotRefToTarget, or pick.n.plot.shape. I’d also generate a hypothetical shape in empty space of the arch to determine whether or not that is even a biologically-viable shape.

Hope this helps,

Dean

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] PLS and CVA
messages.body_plain:
Fatih,

In the geomorph realm, we evaluate angles between vectors using RRPP.  This is a residual permutation procedure, which we used for comparing the angles of vectors for trajectory analysis (e.g., Collyer and Adams 2007); however it has far more uses.

If one has performed PLS in geomorph, then one has the permutation scheme as part of the output object. Using the defaults with 999 iterations of the permutation, there is an object with 1000 elements: the first is the observed. One can take the observed PLS vector and obtain the angle between it and your CVA angle.  Then, set up a loop (or a lapply line) which goes through all 1000 components: the observed vs. CVA and the 999 permuted vs. CVA.  That provides you a distribution from which an effect size (Z-score) and a p-value may be obtained.

Dean

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Interpretation of integration.Vrel output
messages.body_plain:
Madlen,

The short answer is use Z.obs.

ZR (the translated version) is provided as a heuristic for interpretation, as Z.obs ranges from negative to positive values. However, ZR is based on a ‘null’ value, which in turn is based on sample size. Thus, when N is very different between samples it is possible that the order of ZR does not match that of Z.obs.  This is a bit inconvenient in such circumstances, meaning the translated version is not as useful as it is in most other cases. Please take a look at the equations in our 2022 paper for more details.

However, Z.obs remains robust in all cases, and is used in downstream effect size comparisons, so interpret your results based on this.

Hope this helps.

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams (he/him)

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Interpretation of integration.Vrel output

Hello,

I am examining integration in endocranial shape across different clades and having a bit of trouble interpreting the outputs of the integration.Vrel function. From what I understand, a larger effect size of Vrel (Z.obs) indicates a greater degree of integration among traits while ZR is essentially the Z.obs translated to a positive scale so that ZR = 0 represents no integration. Seems fairly straightforward that the ZR should follow the patterns of the Z.obs (I assumed).

However, I have performed five integration tests on clade specific subsets of my Y.gpa$coords data (not performing separate GPA on each clade) and the patterns appear to differ when comparing the Z.obs to the ZR. For instance, according to the Z.obs rodents have the highest degree of integration among these clades while lagomorphs have the least, while according to the ZR lagomorphs have the greatest integration followed by rodents. Is my understanding of what these data mean incorrect or should I not be comparing the results from these separate tests in this way?

When I run this data through the compare.ZVrel function lagomorphs and rodents show significant difference which leads me to believe I should follow the pattern present in the Z.obs.

Results (species per group ranges from n=14 - 71)

                                            Re.obs    Z.obs   ZR            ZR.var
Haplorhini                    0.173   -0.781  0.550   0.067
Lagomorpha                0.339   -0.333  0.883   0.083
Rodentia                              0.079       -1.229  0.874   0.015
Scandentia                  0.111   -1.043  0.123   0.091
Strepsirrhini             0.109       -1.051  0.344   0.059

Kind regards,

Madlen

P.S. Here is an excerpt of my code in case it is useful

coords.hap <- GDF$landmarks[ , , GDF$clade == "Haplorhini"]

int.hap <- integration.Vrel(coords.hap, phy=NULL)

Hello, all
I'm trying to test the correlation of the diet and allometric trajectories of the pitviper skulls, in a phylogenetic context, similar to Esquerré <https://www.jstor.org/action/doBasicSearch?Query=au%3A%22Damien%20Esquerr%C3%A9%22>, et al. 2017  (https://www.jstor.org/stable/48575235?seq=9).
I would like to know how to extract the slope information by species for further procD.pgls analyses or phylogenetic ANCOVA.
I had already run an ANCOVA comparing slopes among species, and pairwise compared it:
HoS_test<-rocD.lm(Sk_shape~Class_Csize$skull_GPA.Csize*Class_Csize$SPECIE,iter=999)
summary(HoS_test)
Pairwise<-pairwise(HoS_test, covariate = Class_Csize$skull_GPA.Csize, groups=Class_Csize$SPECIE)
PW<-summary(Pairwise, test.type = 'var').

Thanks for the attention!

messages.subject: Help interpreting results of physignal and physignal.z
messages.subject_clean: Help interpreting results of physignal and physignal.z
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,
I'm assessing the phylogenetic signal in a genus compose by 6 species using as dataset landmarks taken from skull and mandible in 2D.  I already read the papers that explain the theory behind these two function that assess the signal (Adams 2014, Collyer,Baken& Adams2022.). However, I still don't understand if I am interpreting correctly my results.

I would really appreciate if some of you can help me with the interpretation or suggest me some reading .

Best regards
Julio

Below my results and commented doubts. I'm using the last version of geomorph 4.0.5
# physignal outputs: physignal(A= data, phy= tree, iter=999);
skull dorsal: K = 0.7004 ; P = 0.39085
skull Lateral: K = 0.7883; P = 0.2
skull Ventral: K= 1.0677; P = 0.026
Mandible: K = 1.2769: P= 0.016

Doubt 1. I interpreted that all my datasets have "strong" phylogenetic signal. But only are significant in ventral and mandible. However, I don't undersand why  K values are above 1 in ventral and mandible datasets.

# physignal.z outputs: physignal.z(A = data, phy = tree,
                              lambda = "front", iter=999)
skull Dorsal: Z= 0.22 ; P =0.4925
skull Lateral:
      The scaling parameter, lambda, was optimized at 0.
       This means that the log-likehood was invariant across permutations and there is no  phylogenetic signal in the data.
skull Ventral: Z= 0.1549; P = 0.4885
Mandibula: Z = -0.0857; P= 0.5045

Doubt 2. Why I don't have Z value in lateral dataset?.

Doubt 3. I chose "front" as an option optimization method. However, even after reading the help documentation I don't understand which option is more appropriate for my small tree (6 species) comparison.

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help interpreting results of physignal and physignal.z
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Help interpreting results of physignal and physignal.z
messages.body_plain:
Dear Julio,

> … phylogenetic signal in a genus compose by 6 species using as dataset landmarks taken from skull and mandible in 2D. ..

Any results should be interpreted cautiously with only 6 observations.  There are only so many random permutations that are possible with such a small data set.

>
> Below my results and commented doubts. I'm using the last version of geomorph 4.0.5
> # physignal outputs: physignal(A= data, phy= tree, iter=999);
> skull dorsal: K = 0.7004 ; P = 0.39085
> skull Lateral: K = 0.7883; P = 0.2
> skull Ventral: K= 1.0677; P = 0.026
> Mandible: K = 1.2769: P= 0.016
>
> Doubt 1. I interpreted that all my datasets have "strong" phylogenetic signal. But only are significant in ventral and mandible. However, I don't undersand why  K values are above 1 in ventral and mandible datasets.

I would not interpret “strong” based on K.  Effect sizes are more reliable, as we illustrated in the paper you cited.

>
> # physignal.z outputs: physignal.z(A = data, phy = tree,
>                               lambda = "front", iter=999)
> skull Dorsal: Z= 0.22 ; P =0.4925

For example, this is a small effect size.

> skull Lateral:
>       The scaling parameter, lambda, was optimized at 0.
>        This means that the log-likehood was invariant across permutations and there is no  phylogenetic signal in the data.
> skull Ventral: Z= 0.1549; P = 0.4885
> Mandibula: Z = -0.0857; P= 0.5045
>
> Doubt 2. Why I don't have Z value in lateral dataset?.

The comment you received explains why.  If lambda is optimized at 0 (star phylogeny), then you have no phylogenetic signal, and the log-likelihood would be constant in every random permutation.  The Z-score is NaN because the standard deviation of the null distribution is 0.  There is no effect size to report if lambda = 0.

>
> Doubt 3. I chose "front" as an option optimization method. However, even after reading the help documentation I don't understand which option is more appropriate for my small tree (6 species) comparison.
>

This is maybe a good choice to use if you have more variables than observations, which you probably have.  It concentrates the phylogenetic signal in the fewest dimensions (the first few, i.e., those in front of the others)

There really is no good advice because research in this area is lacking.  Optimizing a parameter like lambda for multivariate data, combined with using RRPP to find effect sizes is not straightforward.  Until more research is performed, we make these options available.  I would probably use “burn” in most cases that would allow it, because it maximizes the effect size rather than log-likelihood.  Thus it finds the lambda where effect size is greatest.  Although effect size and log-likelihood should be correlated, I would prefer to not assume the effect size is maximized where the log-likelihood is maximized, but find the place on the effect-size landscape that it is obviously valid.

However, I am also not so bold as to suggest that maximizing effect size based on RRPP should supplant maximizing likelihood, a technique that has been a basis of inference in many disciplines.  Again, more research is needed.  It does not hurt to try each method and only worry if you get contrasting results, which with 6 observations, you might.

Best,
Mike
